cards.explanation: The city is Ramoth-gilead. In Samaria, Ahab sacrificed many sheep and cattle for Jehoshaphat and the people with him, and urged him to march up to Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 18:2). That's a big welcome with a big ask, friends.

The answer is False. Judah isn't staying out of it. Jehoshaphat tells Ahab, "I am as you are, and my people are your people; we will join you in the war." He doesn't just say yes for himself, he puts his whole people in the boat. That's a big promise to make in one breath.
The missing word is "word." Jehoshaphat says, "Please inquire first for the word of the LORD." He wants to hear from God before anybody marches anywhere. Smart move, friends.

The answer is False. All four hundred prophets say "Go up," and promise that "…God will deliver it into the hand of the king." Not one of them says to hold back. That's the whole room nodding together.

Ahab hates Micaiah because he never prophesies anything good for Ahab. Ahab says it himself: "…I hate him because he never prophesies anything good for me, but only bad." Notice that Ahab's complaint isn't that Micaiah gets it wrong. It's that he doesn't like what he hears. That's a tough way to shop for advice.
The answer is True. When Ahab says he hates Micaiah, Jehoshaphat answers, "The king should not say that!" He doesn't let it slide, even though he's the guest. I'd say that takes some nerve, friends.

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns for himself. He then declares, "With these you shall gore the Arameans until they are finished off." The man showed up with an accessory, friends. I stamp cookies, and even I never brought a prop.

The messenger asks Micaiah to speak favorably like the other prophets. He says the prophets all agree in favor of the king, so "…please let your words be like theirs, and speak favorably." It's a friendly nudge to go along with the crowd. Sounds easy, until you're the one in the room.

The answer is "his God." Micaiah says, "As surely as the LORD lives, I will speak whatever my God tells me." The messenger had just told him the prophets were speaking favorably to the king, and asked him to speak favorably too (2 Chronicles 18:12). Micaiah's words are going to come from his God, friends.

The answer is True, and it's a surprise. Micaiah says, "Go up and triumph…" and adds, "for they will be delivered into your hand." That's the same song the four hundred sang. Hold onto that, friends, because Ahab's about to notice something.

Micaiah pictures all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. He says, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd." It's a hard picture, and I think Ahab felt it.
The answer is True. Micaiah tells what he saw: "And the LORD said, ‘These people have no master; let each one return home in peace.’…" Notice the last part. Home, in peace.
The missing word is "fall." The LORD asks, "Who will entice Ahab king of Israel to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?" Micaiah is describing Ahab's fall, not his victory. That's a heavy one.
The missing word is "lying." The spirit says, "I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets." It's a strange scene, friends, and Micaiah tells it plainly.

Zedekiah demands to know which way the Spirit of the LORD went to reach Micaiah. He strikes Micaiah in the face and demands, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go when He departed from me to speak with you?" He's claiming the Spirit was with him first. It's a hard moment, and I think it hurts to read.

Micaiah says Zedekiah will hide in an inner room. His words are, "You will soon see, on that day when you go and hide in an inner room." Notice who Micaiah says will be hiding. It's the man who just struck him, and Micaiah answers with words.
The answer is False. Ahab says to "…feed him only bread and water until I return safely." Only bread and water. After the feast Ahab threw for Jehoshaphat, that's quite the difference.

Micaiah says that if Ahab returns safely, the LORD has not spoken through him. His words are, "If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me." He puts everything on the line. If Ahab comes home fine, Micaiah is wrong, and he says so out loud.

Ahab tells Jehoshaphat he'll disguise himself while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes. He says, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your royal robes." Think about that, friends. He hides, and his guest stands out in the royal robes.

The missing word is "Israel." The king of Aram orders his chariot commanders, "Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel." Aram was the nation Ahab was fighting. Only one target on the list, and that's Ahab's crown.

Jehoshaphat cries out and the LORD helps him. The text says, "…Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God drew them away from him." He's in the royal robes with chariots turning toward him, and he cries out. That's a good thing to do when you're in trouble, friends.
The answer is False. The commanders "…saw that he was not the king of Israel…" and "…they turned back from pursuing him." Wrong king, case closed. They had one target, and it wasn't Jehoshaphat.

Ahab tells his charioteer to turn around and take him out of the battle. He says, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, for I am badly wounded!" The arrow hit between the joints of his armor. Friends, even a disguise couldn't hide him from that.
The answer is True. The text says, "…at sunset he died." That's the end of Ahab, and it's a sobering line. I think this one is heavy, friends.
